claim: The core library is the product; the CLI is an add-on.
why: The product is the protocol, its vectors and one implementation. Other languages meet it at the JSON format, the CLI or a socket. Lean on existing standards wherever one fits.

claim: Rust, in a new strange-loops repo.
why: Historical plan: a core crate, a CLI crate, and adjacent Lean model, vectors and scenarios enforce budgets. Version 31 chose Rust for phones and browser extensions. Version 35 removed the Go core (PR 6) while model boundaries were reviewed. Rust is now implemented in rust/, with a pure core and a fixture evaluator. JS and Rust check all protocol fixture families and external standards. Product CLI, storage and budget tooling remain planned. The proposed .loops/ migration remains a collector in the old repo.

claim: One word per concept, one concept per word.
why: The Glossary lists the vocabulary. Record replaces fact. Anchor, thing, place and realm absorb genesis, subject, residence and topology. Seal retires: observers emit, vertices tick and ticks cover records. Normative prose lives in the protocol. LatestBy replaces Upsert. Vertex stays: it is where loops meet.

claim: A store is a set, not a sequence.
why: Receipt order leaves the fold. Underneath: immutable single-writer segments, content-addressed blobs, a derived index.

claim: Every record has an observer, and two times.
why: Ingestion is a dumb observer reporting what a source holds: hearsay. emitted is the writer's word (RFC 3339); occurred is an optional claimed span that can be coarse.

claim: occurred is a span with a closed grammar: dates, instants and intervals, never a duration.
why: Each occurred value names one span. Content order reads that span; future windows use its start. Calendar dates are UTC days. EDTF Level 1 qualifiers (2009~) and trailing unspecified digits (201X) retain one span. Qualifiers never change it. Intervals join two points and may have an open end (2019/..). Spans order by start, then end, with open ends last. Content order compares span, emitted, then id digest bytes, never spellings. Without occurred, a record has its emitted instant span. Base32 text order differs from digest-byte order. Durations repeat what an end instant says. Seasons, open or unknown starts, unknown ends and years past 9999 fail with occurred-not-span. Accepting less would invalidate stored records. Version 35.

claim: Identity is a content hash; signatures sit beside it.
why: A salted payload commitment, an id over the canonical {commit, env}, an Ed25519 signature over loops/record/v1: plus the id. References stay opaque. Records are signed by default and a store carries its writers' key bindings, so it verifies itself. The version in the signed prefix lets a reader refuse only what is newer than it knows.

claim: Writing the same record twice is a no-op.
why: A record's id covers its envelope, including emitted, plus its salt and payload. The same draft written twice is the same record, and set union absorbs it, in a batch or across batches. A new observation gets a fresh salt, so it gets a new id and is simply a new record. Version 35.

claim: A record erases through its envelope field erases; any kind may erase.
why: erases is a set of record ids, refused unless each is one, and never a label. It sits on the envelope, so every reader applies it, whatever its grant. Targets in about were rejected: about: [r:X] already names the thing X anchors, which holds X's revisions too, and a kind would decide which reading applied. No kind is reserved for erasing, so the field carries the meaning by itself, and a revision can erase what it replaces: prev: [r:X], erases: [r:X]. Authority keys on the field. Version 35.

claim: A field belongs on the envelope only if the core reads it.
why: The envelope holds kind, observer, emitted, optional occurred, about, prev, under and erases. derived-from, seen and refs belong in payloads. Readers refuse unknown envelope fields.

claim: A payload is here, withheld or erased; supersession reads only the envelope.
why: prev sits on the envelope. Withholding or erasing payloads preserves each thing's head ids. A record superseded within a thing cannot become current there. A payload test answers unknown when its payload is unavailable. Results count covered records they cannot read. Added in version 32.

claim: Erasure is per store and small; privacy is withholding, not hiding.
why: Erasure removes payloads but keeps commitments and ids. Consistent forms determine one settled record per id, independent of read order. A reader keeps a held payload unless a held eraser names its id. A bare erased copy cannot suppress a held payload. Disclosure splits by kind when recording. Planned disclosure keeps derived data under its least-public input's grant.

claim: Writers bound every number’s magnitude; numeric readers additionally require whole values.
why: RFC 8785 reads numbers as binary64 before canonicalization. The final 13:25 human ruling keeps Option A: writers refuse any magnitude above 253−1, whole or not (number-out-of-range); 1e30 is refused. Within-range fractions are accepted. Numeric readers additionally require whole values. Exact decimal or large-integer values belong in strings.

claim: One checked write path, and what it returns carries the proof.
why: write checks the envelope, salt length, repeated members at any depth, then nonfinite numbers or any number outside ±(253−1), whole or not. Within-range fractions pass. A batch uses the same path, with refusal priority independent of draft order and prev order. It returns a Written record carrying the proof, including distinct member names. Version 35 (PR 7), with the final 13:25 writer-range ruling.

claim: Observers are things, with lineages under their names.
why: A lineage id is the hash of its anchor. Names, keys and models are records about a lineage. Names never take part in matching: they resolve at read, through name tables and @home.

claim: Naming, key binding and authority stay separate.
why: Authority is a grant record, pointed to by under. One stance shape covers affirm, adopt, dispute, retire and authorize. A delegate is a shared seat; an identity that emerges starts its own lineage and adopts what it wants to own.

claim: A label may stand in under.
why: A changeset can create grant @g and act under it. under accepts labels, like about and prev, and participates in cycle detection. Historical standing plan: it names a grant held in the batch or store. Future standing checks decide whether that grant authorizes the act. A label grants no extra authority. Version 35.

claim: Keys in tiers, and presence for what takes effect.
why: A lineage pins its root key. The standing plan gives each device presence and emit keys; agents receive session keys. Effective authority changes require a person present. A grant records presence ahead of time: agents propose and narrow, never widen. Standing ends by retirement through held records, never by time.

claim: Identity lives in the record, in about.
why: A thing uses an anchor record id or a typed natural key computed by tooling, such as a URL or code birth key. The core compares those references. Observers and stores use proposed reserved *-anchor kinds. A vertex instead hashes its canonical spec and parameters; it has no anchor or standing. Proposed equivalence, provenance and succession remain separate; resolve-by joins identities at read. Unknown names follow the planned store maturity rules.

claim: A facet is one kind about one thing, emitted whole.
why: Current state is LatestBy per thing; from then chooses kinds. prev is a set, so forks retain several heads. Links are new records, never edits to about. A record about several things belongs to each, but a successor may replace it within only some. A record about nothing anchors its own thing by id. Its revision names that id in about, so unrelated empty-about records never fork each other. Version 35.

claim: prev is succession within a thing.
why: Within a fixed admitted set, succession affects only shared things. Writers refuse unheld prev targets outside the batch (prev-unknown) and unrelated targets (prev-unrelated). Readers reject held unrelated targets, but admit unknown targets because they cannot judge them. Planned moving or narrowing uses explicit retire records. Replacement rules read only envelopes; future standing supplies authority. Version 34.

claim: A vertex is a question; a store is a thing you write into.
why: A vertex owns no storage or sources. Its id hashes its canonical spec and parameters; a name record points to the current id. It has no anchor, key or standing. Equal specs and parameters name the same vertex wherever evaluated (version 32). The store plan uses lineage declarations and machine-local places. Dated declarations accrete without migrations; admission enforces maturity.

claim: Specs are JSON, stored as records.
why: protocol/spec.md is normative; protocol/schema.md and JSON Schema files do not exist. The storage plan uses vertex records and note comments. Parameterized templates remain proposed. The core accepts supported specs as data. Every accepted spec has at least one source; absent or empty from fails with from-missing.

claim: Six folds in two families, plus modifiers.
why: Count, Sum, Min, Max, LatestBy and Collect form the supported fold vocabulary. Supported modifiers follow protocol/spec.md. Historical proposals include by, order, set mode, windows and ranking-only weight-by; they are not implemented grammar. The proposed Avg lens divides Sum by Count. With each input id supplied once, commuting accumulators and over-head folds obey their set laws. Incremental over-head evaluation needs cached LatestBy state, not merely a cached answer. Max's scalar state cannot track changing heads; this proves no impossibility for all bounded-state algorithms. JS and Rust sums use unbounded integers. Future bounded ports must refuse overflow. Version 32.

claim: Predicates are a closed, typed set.
why: Six where operators test individual records. Future boundaries can test vertex state. No regex, arithmetic, user code or effects: an observer records classifications instead. Proposed collectors own parse pipelines; future boundaries omit run hooks.

claim: where can test any envelope field, named explicitly.
why: Envelope tests use env.kind, env.observer, env.emitted, env.occurred, env.about, env.prev, env.under and env.erases. Bare names identify payload fields. Unknown env. names are refused. Arguments must fit their fields: typed references, record ids, times, or supported payload scalars. Numeric tests require safe whole values after binary64 ingestion. Numeric complement laws additionally require a numeric bound. Missing and nonwhole values need not pass either bound. Time equality compares spans, not spelling; time bounds compare starts. Envelope tests select after supersession. A record without occurred passes neither time bound. The future window plan instead uses its emitted. Windows include starts at their lower bound and exclude starts at their upper bound. The supersession policy within windows remains open. Filtering before supersession could revive replaced records. Whole-span bounds were rejected: January ends before its year despite their equal starts. Observer tests use lineage ids until name tables arrive. Specs refuse repeated keys and empty where maps. Latest-by explicitly requires "follow": "prev". Version 35.

claim: unread counts what couldn't be read.
why: A covered record is unread when its payload test is unknown or its selected numeric fold cannot read a safe whole field. Count each id once per slot, including records that head several things. Collect counts unknown candidates before its limit. Full-result equality needs answering tests and fold-readable covered records. Historical version 35 counted only uncertainty affecting the limit and overclaimed unread: 0. PR 13 removed those claims. A stronger limit-sensitive guarantee remains future work, not a current theorem.

claim: Supersession runs over everything held; selection comes after.
why: Each thing's state uses its records from the fixed admitted set, before vertex selection. from, envelope tests and payload tests then choose among heads. Selecting first could revive a record superseded by another kind, an excluded source, a failed filter or a withheld successor. Count and sum include selected history, even when superseded. Found while modelling the spec (versions 33 and 34).

claim: A tick is a value; a stored tick is a signed record.
why: Future tick design: a content tick hashes its vertex, covered ids and result. Machines with the same inputs can recompute that id. Persistence uses an ordinary tick record signed by its writer, preserving one envelope. A witness tick records the runner's observed set. Erased numeric inputs leave only the signature as evidence for prior results. Proposed revisits create ticks citing earlier ticks. These transitions are not implemented proofs. Version 32.

claim: Every result has two names.
why: Future build design: results have an input key and result hash. Downstream keys use result hashes, so unchanged results stop work. Incremental commuting folds need accumulator state; over-head folds need LatestBy state. Cached result values alone are insufficient.

claim: State references form a DAG; ticks may loop.
why: Future state references form an acyclic dependency graph. Tick feedback crosses explicit recorded steps. Hygiene vertices would expose drift and self-reinforcing salience. Reference, boundary and tick transitions still need models and proofs.

claim: A place is a location, a format and a scope.
why: Roles are write, hold and blobs: JSONL where git needs it, SQLite where volume does. The index is derived and disposable.

claim: Replication is set union by segment lists.
why: A segment closes once committed, so branches only add files, and a committed segment changing outside an erase is the alarm. A static place is closed segments named by hash plus one mutable segments.json.

claim: A realm is the stores its root name table reaches.
why: Membership is a link, not containment. Across realms: compose by default, bridge only as an explicit signed tick, never replicate. A public store is a standing bridge, declared with presence.

claim: Federation is each person's own store, plus composition.
why: Replies carry the thread's root in about; a ping says only where to look. Admission filters and weight ranks.

claim: A lens is a collector with a base.
why: Render roundtrip requires nonempty, distinct section ids. Put-get additionally requires distinct base ids and the exact same ordered id list in the edit. A dropped section retains its old body. The broader lens plan records a base of tick, lens hash and audience. It renders, parses edits, diffs by id and emits a changeset. Committed renders are promotions. One tick can have several renders. Absence is never an edit. Anything an observer writes remains its own record.

claim: Context travels by tick.
why: Proposed context design: references have five states: here, fetchable, withheld, erased or unreachable. Bundles carry what the receiver cannot fetch, filtered by its grant. A session witness tick records known ids and supports key retirement. A brief cites a signed tick record. A cloud run borrows a place and syncs at each tick. These transitions remain future work.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: One API under every surface.
why: Planned API: pure functions and a realm handle that narrows grants, never widens them. Identity-aware reads use fold; tick and witness match the two proposed tick forms. Refusals have closed codes. Future serve JSON-RPC mirrors the crate for LSP, MCP and front ends.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: No subscriptions, no coordinator.
why: A watcher owns its checkpoint. Future boundaries run where the handle receives records. Content ticks can run anywhere with matching inputs; witness ticks need their signing key. Boundary and tick transition proofs remain future work.

group: The local API and its surfaces
claim: The CLI is verb first, with the API's verbs.
why: Proposed CLI: HTTPie-style payload syntax and JSON shared with serve. It has no zoom flags. Core batches already check labels; product atomic storage remains planned.

claim: The limits, in four tiers.
why: Not the model, not in the core, not yet (each with a trigger), outside by design. Something enters the core only if two separate cases need it and it can't be built from records, ticks and lenses. No state-machine framework: each vertex already is one.

claim: Budgets guard failures, not size.
why: Tokens per module, public API snapshots, vocabulary prices, dependency allowlists and inward layering define the budget plan. A budget increase needs a ledger entry citing the core rule. The Go budget checker left with the Go core. Rust exists now; the proposed xtask budget tool remains unimplemented.

claim: Model laws and external checks guide Rust; the workspace also has characterization tests.
why: The historical plan rejected unit tests in favor of proofs, vectors, differential fuzzing and scenarios. Rust now has public fixture tests, standards checks and characterization tests. The Lean model computes protocol-vector answers; separate theorem files prove the listed laws. External standards supply their own expected data. The intended rule remains: do not derive expected answers from the implementation under test.

claim: A law counts only where its boundary establishes its hypotheses.
why: The fold laws held. What failed were the boundaries: a law assumed distinct ids or distinct member names, and nothing guaranteed them. Parsing, writing and settling return types that carry their invariants, as Written does, and the laws take those types. Version 35.

claim: An outside review at each modelling step.
why: A reviewer from another lab gets the code and the docs, never our conclusions. Each finding becomes a vector, a theorem or a narrower claim. Codex found three of our five findings on its own and eight more besides.

claim: Rust now implements the modeled protocol; product storage and higher transitions remain planned.
why: The model proves LatestBy's set law and Count's repeat behavior under their stated premises. Lens render laws require valid ids; put-get also preserves the exact ordered id list. Layer 0 vectors compare modeled, JS and Rust bytes. Hash-parametric laws cover erasure, sets and member order. Step 2 introduced distinct-id fold families, per-thing heads, consistent-form settling, honest unread results, spec parsing and at-most-one batch meaning. Historical boundary reviews produced PRs 7 and 9–13. PR 7 checks writing; PR 9 adds erases; PR 10 preserves unneeded backslashes. PR 11 defines occurred grammar; PR 12 orders real times and digest bytes. PR 13 extends envelope tests and defines the normative spec grammar. Its historical snapshot had 171 vectors. The law catalogue lists 72 entries across 606 theorem declarations. Fixture counts change with the integration campaign; consult the final campaign report. Rust checks all families and standards. Current writers cap every number's magnitude at 253 − 1, whole or not. Numeric folds additionally require safe whole values. Ticks, references, boundaries and storage transitions still need future models and proofs.

claim: The design page is built from the repo.
why: Its sections are HTML and its ledger is these records, in design/rethink/. node design/build.mjs renders the page, CI checks the render, projects.gruel.world serves it unlisted, and the claude.ai artifact is a mirror. Once .loops/ exists, the ledger is read from it. Version 35.
